    PATIENCE SHANKLIN ESTATE TRUST AND THE BRANDON SHANKLIN TRUST
                      INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

           COMES NOW Patience Shanklin Estate Trust and the Brandon Shanklin Trust, in the

above-styled case, and pursuant to SOAH Order No. 19, 1 files this Initial Post-Hearing Brief and

would like to show the following:

                                   INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY

           Patience Shanklin Estate Trust and the Brandon Shanklin Trust submit this Initial Post-

Hearing Brief in Docket No. 59475 in opposition of any route utilizing in order of priority Link

J24, Link J25, Link J27, and Link J8, and in support of any route not utilizing Link J24, Link J25,

Link J27, and Link J8, e.g., Route 487, the route selected by the Public Utility Commission

(“PUC”), best satisfies PURA and the Commission’s routing criteria. 2


1
    SOAH Order No. 32 at 2, PUC No. 59475 H’rg (filed on the Interchange on Jun. 15, 2026).
2
 See Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. No. 23, PUC No. 59475 H’rg (providing the route ID & link sequence description for

{1753/008/00308852.DOCX;2 }                              1
                                                ARGUMENT

          Routes that do not utilize Link J24, Link J25, Link J27, and Link J8 best meet routing

criteria.

          Both Applicant and PUC’s recommended routes mirror each other from the Bell County

East substation west to the Link J10/H1 node, then split with the PUC’s recommended route going

to the north along Links J10, J11, J12, and J13 and Applicant’s preferred route going to the south

along Links H1, H41, H42, J21, J22, J23, J27, and J4, before reconnecting at the Link J13/J4 node

to continue west along identical links for over forty (40) miles through San Saba and McCulloch

Counties, Texas before splitting again at the Link M12/M7 node and then coming together a final

time at the N3/O3/P2/01 node to resume their identical course west to the Big Hill Substation. 3

This brief will focus on the distinction between the PUC and Applicant’s recommended routes

between the Link J10/H1 node and the Link J13/J4 node (“Eastern Split”).

          The use of Routes which include Link J24, Link J25, Link J27, and Link J8 are a far more

burdensome approach to achieving the primary objective of the project. Under Section 25.101 of

the Texas Administrative Code, “[a]n application for a new transmission line must address the

criteria in PURA §37.056(c) and considering those criteria, engineering constraints, and costs, the

line must be routed to the extent reasonable to moderate the impact on the affected community and

landowners.” 4 The use of Link J11 or other more northern links that are superior in cost, length,

engineering constraints and minimize agricultural impact and visibility best accomplish these

considerations. 5

whole, the factors set forth in PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and in 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B).”).

            Cost.

           For the Eastern Split, utilizing the PUC’s Route 487 is $9 million less expensive than

Applicant’s Route 894. 6 Routing the transmission line south to the H Links alone triples the length

and adds at least $7 million in cost. 7 Oncor’s Transmission Engineering Manager Corin E. Cooley

testified that, “[g]enerally, the larger the angle, the greater the associated cost.” 8 Later during cross-

examination, she further acknowledged that, although other factors such as overall line length and

location also influence cost, “adding turning locations does increase cost.” 9 The PUC’s Eastern

Split has only 14 angles on four links compared to Applicant’s Eastern Split having 26 angles on

eight links. For Link J22 on the Applicant’s Eastern Split, at least three hard angles are required to

cross the Colorado River and the accompanying sensitive riparian areas. Whereas the PUC’s

Eastern Split crossing of the Colorado on Link J11 does not require any hard angles. 10 The PUC’s

Eastern Split is also 9.2% shorter than Applicant’s Eastern Split. 11 Increases in distance from these

additional links—when applied across large-scale transmission projects—compound into

substantially greater land use, environmental disturbance, and long-term operational impact across

a multiplied number of affected property owners.

           The cost estimates for the Applicant’s proposed alternative routes cannot be guaranteed.

The cost estimates not only inherently include a contingency that may result in increases of

approximately 10–15%, 12 but the Applicant’s analysis and recommendations fail to account for

           Route 487 best satisfies the Commission’s routing criteria.

          The PUC’s Eastern Split is a record-supported superior route to routes that utilize Link J24,

Link J25, Link J27, and Link J8. Route 487 adheres to the principle that a route must be supported

by evidence of cost, feasibility, and its effect on the routing criteria under PURA § 37.056 and 16

TAC § 25.101. 40 The record reaffirms how Route 487 preserves Route 894’s most favorable

attributes while removing the issues created by the inclusion of Link J27 and replacing it with

Links J11 and J12’s superior corridor utilization, reduced fragmentation, avoidable impacts to

ranch infrastructure and water resources, all while maintaining engineering feasibility and

lowering cost by $16.1 million. 41

          At 221.5 miles, Route 487 is only 7.1 miles longer and 1.7% more costly than the shortest

and least expensive routes. 42 Furthermore, Route 487 has the lowest length in proximity to parks

recreational areas, agricultural cropland with mobile irrigation systems, woodlands, cropland,

rangeland, streams, habitats of federally listed endangered or threated species, areas of

archaeological and historical significance, commercial/industrial areas, private airstrips, FAA-

registered airports within 10,000 feet, heliports, and commercial AM radio transmitters. 43 Route

487 has a greater milage paralleling existing compatible rights-of-way than does Applicant’s Route

894—which aids in reducing costs, is better for the landowner, and was a recommendation that

Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD) suggested to minimize habitat fragmentation. 44

impacts in the impacted areas. 46

           Route selection analysis requires a careful balancing of all considerations in PURA and the

Commission rules, “not simply counting which route performs best in the most individual

metrics.” 47 Accordingly, significant weight should not be placed on the fact that Route 894

performs greater as to habitable structures, as the difference is only 11% and the performance of

Route 487 remains overall superior. The Applicant’s witnesses have made it clear that although

habitable structures are considered, “[t]his does not mean that a proposed transmission line must

avoid habitable structures at all costs, but that reasonable alternatives should be considered.” 48

           Oncor’s CNN Project Specialist, Casey Petty, recommended that “the Commission

consider the 121 additional alternative routes” not just the Applicant’s preferred Route 894. 49

Additionally, Ms. Perkins testified that “all 122 filed routes are acceptable,” and that “it’s up to

the Commission to consider which route they deem considering all the factors.” 50 Route 487 was

           Given these considerations, with its lower projected costs and more robust Environmental

Assessment data, Route 487 stands out as the more prudent and well-substantiated option.

           Patience Shanklin Estate Trust and the Brandon Shanklin Trust oppose any routes

utilizing Link J24, J25, Link J27, and Link J8.

Link J24, Link J25, Link J27, and Link J8, because of their significant impact to the Patience

Shanklin Estate Trust and the Brandon Shanklin Trust’s unique riparian property.

           A transmission line built on Link J24, Link J25, Link J27, and Link J8 would bisect

Patience Shanklin Estate Trust and the Brandon Shanklin Trust’s properties, adversely impacting

not only the farming and ranching operations, but causing such significant damage as to transform

the very topographical diversity that gives the property its environmental significance. 54 The

disturb water drainage patterns, affecting forage quality.

patterns depend on undisturbed surroundings and tall natural vantage points. 62 The installation

process—requiring clearing and heavy equipment— fragments habitats and introduces long-term

disturbances that threaten local biodiversity. The presence of large transmission structures and

power lines increases the risk of collisions and electrocution for birds, directly endangering

populations that are already carefully managed. The Applicant’s proposal to relocate bald eagles

and other migratory birds is not a valid or effective management strategy. 63 Due to their strong site

fidelity, territorial behavior, and legal protections, these species cannot be successfully displaced

without significant risk of harm or displacement-related impacts.               For these reasons, the

environmentally sensitive and wildlife-rich areas found along Link J24, Link J25, Link J27, and

Link J8 are fundamentally unsuitable locations for transmission line development, and routes that

avoid Link J24, Link J25, Link J27, and Link J8 should be prioritized.

boxes in the ranch with existing transmission lines making it unsafe to operate equipment and

detrimental to the agricultural, wildlife, and conservation purposes of the ranch.

 Post-Hearing Brief in Docket No. 59475 in strong opposition to any route that in order of priority

utilizes Link J24, Link J25, Link J27, and Link J8, to include Applicant’s preferred Route 894.

Patience Shanklin Estate Trust and the Brandon Shanklin Trust, support any Route that does not

utilize Link J24, Link J25, Link J27, and Link J8, e.g., the PUC’s recommended Route 487. The

record does not support that Route 894 provides superior overall balancing of the Commission’s

routing criteria relative to Route 487. Importantly, Route 487 achieves these improvements while

remaining identical to Route 894 across approximately 60% of the Project. Route 487 preserves

much of Route 894’s broader framework while materially improving compatible corridor

utilization and reducing fragmentation impacts across the eastern portion of the Project. Patience
